Cslib.SharedMemory.ComplexityHierarchy.theorem_8_8 (n : ℕ) [NeZero n] (hn : 2 ≤ n) : ∃ V v₀ L I, (∀ (i : Fin (n - 1)), I.memInit i = v₀) ∧ (∀ (p : Fin n) (x : (Cslib.SharedMemory.taskObj (Fin n) (Fin n)).Op), I.allowed p x) ∧ Cslib.SharedMemory.Impl.Solves (Cslib.SharedMemory.consensus (Fin n) (Fin n)) I ∧ I.ObstructionFree**Theorem 8.8** of [EGSZ16] (Ellen–Gelashvili–Shavit–Zhu, *A Complexity-Based Hierarchy for Multiprocessor Synchronization*, PODC 2016): there is an obstruction-free protocol for consensus among `n` processes (inputs and decisions in `Fin n`) that uses only `n − 1` memory locations supporting `read` and `swap` (`rswapObj V v₀`, all initially `v₀`). Agreement and (strong) validity hold in every finite execution (`Impl.Solves (consensus …)`), and the protocol is obstruction-free from every reachable configuration (`Impl.ObstructionFree`). The protocol is Algorithm 1 (`swapAlg`), with scans implemented by double collect; the swap arguments carry the process identifier and a sequence number (as in the paper), so the protocol is anonymous only in the sense that identifiers are used for nothing but these tags. Stated for `n ≥ 2` (for `n = 1` there are no locations).

It represents a contradiction. `False` elimination rule, `False.rec`, expresses the fact that anything follows from a contradiction. This rule is sometimes called ex falso (short for ex falso sequitur quodlibet), or the principle of explosion. The target type is actually `C : Sort u` which means it works for both propositions and types. When executed, this acts like an "unreachable" instruction: it is **undefined behavior** to run, but it will probably print "unreachable code". List.{u} (α : Type u) : Type uLinked lists: ordered lists, in which each element has a reference to the next element. Most operations on linked lists take time proportional to the length of the list, because each element must be traversed to find the next element. `List α` is isomorphic to `Array α`, but they are useful for different things: * `List α` is easier for reasoning, and `Array α` is modeled as a wrapper around `List α`. * `List α` works well as a persistent data structure, when many copies of the tail are shared. When the value is not shared, `Array α` will have better performance because it can do destructive updates.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is definitionally equal to that type. 849:
Decidable (p : Prop) : TypeA `Bool` (that is, `decide p`) paired with a proof of `p` if `decide p` is `true` or a proof of `¬p` if `decide p` is `false`. The easiest way to extract these proofs is to use `of_decide_eq_true` or `of_decide_eq_false`. `Decidable` instances are primarily used via `if`-expressions and the tactic `decide`. In conditional expressions, the `Decidable` instance for the proposition is used to select a branch. At run time, this case distinction code is identical to that which would be generated for a `Bool`-based conditional. In proofs, the tactic `decide` synthesizes an instance of `Decidable p`, attempts to reduce `decide p` to `true`, and then succeeds with the proof `of_decide_eq_true rfl` if it can. Because `Decidable` carries data, when writing `@[simp]` lemmas which include a `Decidable` instance on the LHS, it is best to use `{_ : Decidable p}` rather than `[Decidable p]` so that non-canonical instances can be found via unification rather than instance synthesis.
